events.credibility_reason: 33-day-old single-author preprint by an unidentified author, proof developed with substantial AI help, no public expert check; the Lean formalisation covers only the superpattern half, not the reduction to planar-graph point sets; and it claims near-linear superpatterns for the full 213-avoiding class where the 2013 route gave only quadratic ones. No specific error identified, so not set aside.
events.ai_basis: GPT-6 Astra assisted in developing the construction and proof.

why: The statement asks only whether subquadratic universal point sets exist for planar graphs, so Gordon's claimed n^(1+o(1)) explicit construction answers it in full (whole), as the guidelines' own example says. It is unreviewed: no named human checked it, and the sorry-free Lean build covers the superpattern half only (F7). I rated it doubtful, not not_credible: the doubts are real (unknown author, no uptake yet, departs from the known method, the reduction is not formalised), but 33 days is too short for silence to count against it and no error has been identified. AI role is assisted, not generated: the introduction says the work started 'from the author's interval-based approach' and the model 'helped develop the construction, formulate and revise the proof', so the model contributed mathematics inside a human-led result. The pre-snapshot class-restricted subquadratic or linear constructions are cases with journal or refereed-conference digestion. Bannister et al. is scored as a case for its near-linear bounded-pathwidth result; its general n^2/4 bound is not subquadratic. Scheucher et al.'s linear lower bound is a bound. Cardinal et al.'s exact-size results and Gavoille-Jacques's induced-universal graphs are variants.
doubts: Gordon's AI quotes came through summarising fetches with quote limits; the exact wording is unconfirmed against the full text. The repository commit history was not seen, so an earlier public date for Gordon cannot be ruled out, though any such date would still fall after the snapshot. Close call on Bannister et al.: case (bounded-pathwidth near-linear sets) versus bound (n^2/4). Pre-snapshot digestion rests on journal publication reported in search summaries, not on opened pages.
